content: A rhombus, in the field of geometry, is defined as an equilateral parallelogram. This means it is a four-sided polygon where all sides are of equal length. The term rhombus originates from the Ancient Greek word ῥόμβος (rhombos), which translates to spinning top. The plural forms of rhombus are rhombi or rhombuses, and it is sometimes referred to as a rhomb. Informally, it is often called a diamond, as seen in the diamond suit of playing cards, or a lozenge, due to the resemblance of these shapes to rhombi. However, not all rhombi are necessarily diamonds or lozenges. A rhombus is a specific type of quadrilateral, and when a rhombus has right angles, it is classified as a square. The area of a rhombus can be calculated using several methods. One method involves the product of the lengths of its diagonals, divided by two: Area = (D₁ × D₂) / 2, where D₁ and D₂ are the lengths of the diagonals. Since a rhombus is also a parallelogram, its area can alternatively be determined by multiplying the length of one side (B) by the perpendicular distance (H) between two opposite sides: Area = B × H. Another formula for the area involves the square of the side length (a) multiplied by the sine of any interior angle (θ): Area = a² × sin(θ), where a represents the side length, and θ is the angle between two adjacent sides. The diagonals of a rhombus are always perpendicular to each other. This property can be proven mathematically. If the vertices of the rhombus are labeled as A, B, C, and D, and vectors are used to represent the sides and diagonals, the relationships between these vectors can be analyzed. For example, the vector from A to C can be expressed as the sum of the vectors from A to B and B to C. Similarly, the vector from B to D can be expressed as the difference between the vectors from B to C and A to B, due to the parallelism of opposite sides. By taking the inner product of the diagonal vectors, it can be shown that the inner product equals zero if and only if the diagonals are perpendicular. This result follows from the bilinear and symmetric properties of the inner product, as well as the equality of the side lengths. Rhombi can also be used in tiling patterns, a concept known as tessellation, where the shape is repeated without gaps or overlaps to cover a plane. The term rhombus has its origins in the Greek language, where it referred to something that spins. The Greek mathematician Euclid used the word ῥόμβος (rhombos), derived from the verb ρέμβω (rhembo), meaning to turn round and round. Archimedes, another prominent Greek mathematician, used the term solid rhombus to describe a geometric figure formed by two right circular cones sharing a common base.
